Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is my game of the year for 2025. 
I have played the original game and have also really enjoyed it, so this is not the first time that I’m exploring Medieval Europe as Henry of Skalitz. 

Since first playing KC:D II on the day, it was released on February 4th, 2025, I have been playing it all year. The 145+ hours that I played it was on just one playthrough, so you know this game has a lot of content. 

This game features a beautiful large open world to explore with the help of your trusty steed full of historical Medieval landmarks in the Kingdom of Bohemia. As someone who has visited Czechia during the 21st century not 15th century. I don’t have access to a time machine…Yet. 😊 Warhorse Studios did a great job capturing the feel of Czechia’s countryside. Many fans have visited locations from the game and compared them with real life. 
Here is an example of Trosky castle which plays a role in the game’s story.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3526530836

Speaking of time machines, the game’s soundtrack is very appropriate and gives you the feeling that you have traveled back in time to the Middle Ages. Warhorse Studios spared no expense and had an Orchestra perform some of the games most memorable music. 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u23H6aqhuSQ

Regarding the gameplay itself, it feels like the first game but more streamlined and simplified compared to the first game. I still find it highly enjoyable!
Even if it is simplified by the standards of the first game, I still found the combat in this game is still much better than in most action RPGs that use Medieval inspired weapons that I have played. After experiencing combat in KC:D II, I found it hard to go back to other action RPGs that focus on combat with swords and other weapons that you would find during the Middle Ages. Games which still use simpler “hack and slash” style gameplay which just requires you to click your left mouse button repeatedly instead of the more complex and realistic combat mechanics that requires more practice like KC:D II has. 

Combat is not the only part of the game, KC:D II is a story driven RPG in the truest sense. I will not post any spoilers but the games story and especially the ending does a fantastic job of concluding the story of Henry of Skalitz. Even half a year after finishing the main quest I found the ending very satisfying and is still in my memory. 

Interesting fact, the games script has over 2.2 million words, making it the longest script in video game history! Talk about a milestone for gaming as a form of sophisticated storytelling. 

https://www.gamesradar.com/games/rpg/kingdom-come-deliverance-2-devs-boast-of-a-2-2-million-word-script-that-would-break-baldurs-gate-3s-world-record-and-larians-publishing-director-says-i-hope-they-do/

Overall, I think that this game stands out from the rest of the RPGs on the market. In an industry where it feels like we have a sea of RPGs with fantasy settings it is refreshing to see a more realistic game that explores real historical locations. I hope the industry takes notice and more role-playing games with historical settings are released. For the Czechia-based Warhorse Studios making a game about their nation’s Medieval history was obviously a labor of love and it shows in the finale product.

If you are interested in the Middle Ages and like action RPGs this is not a game, you should miss playing.  
Whatever game wins GOTY on Steam this year Kingdom Come: Deliverance II will be the game of the year for me.

There are so many things I love about this game, but many other reviewers have already gone into great depth about its many amazing qualities, so I'm not going to repeat them much here. Instead I am going to address some criticisms I see (and sometimes agree with), but also address why those criticisms shouldn't prevent you from playing this great game. 

One criticism I see and that I agree with is that the requirement of brewing potions in order to save your game outside of save points can be annoying. Luckily there is a way to get around this requirement. After installing the game, go to your steam library, right click on KCD2, and select "properties." Then, in the properties window go to "launch options," and add the command "-devmode" (not including quotation marks). Now, whenever you launch the game, press the tilde key (~) and enter the command "wh_sys_nosavepotion 1" (not including quotation marks), and now you will be able to save your game without needing a saviors schnapps potion. 

Another complaint that I see is that the combat is annoyingly difficult. I agree that its difficult, but I don't think its annoyingly so. In my experience most RPGs fall into one of two combat formats. The first category would be games like Assassin's Creed and Witcher 3, where where one button attacks, another blocks, and maybe one dodges. The second category is souls-like combat where you have to be super strategic and any mistakes are punished harshly. The KCD franchise doesn't fit into either of those categories. This might not be the best way to describe it, but I'd describe it as needing more real-time combat strategy. Button mashing won't get you anywhere because if you keep doing the same thing your opponents will learn your pattern and block it. Unlike souls-like games where you have to plan your combat in advance and learn an enemy's patterns, in KCD you have to be continuously watching your enemy to see which attacks and strategies they favor, but also how they respond to your attacks and strategies. Its an innovative system which I think makes combat more engaging than in games like Witcher 3, and difficult in a way which I appreciate more than souls-like combat. 

A third complaint I see with irritating frequency is that certain people don't like that there are Jewish characters and the option for a same-sex romance in this game. They seem to think by including that the devs are putting modern politics into the middle ages and breaking immersion or some other such nonsense. Judaism has existed in Europe for longer than Christianity has, and there have been LGBTQ+ people for just as long as there have been straight people. If that's a deal breaker for you then I'm not going to try to argue with you, and please don't try to argue with me.

They have taken everything that was cool, and made it 100 times better. I am so f**king happy after playing this and I'm still thoroughly addicted. The music is amazing, world and exploration is breathtaking. I cannot praise it enough. It was so worth the wait, and it's making me so excited for the future. I'm just so damn happy Warhorse made this game. It puts Bethesda (who I love) to shame in so many ways. I played Skyrim often for a decade, I see myself playing this for far longer.

I love so so much about it, I love its commitment to realism and aversion to fantasy (I love fantasy, but the hard commitment to realism is a breath of fresh air). I love the character writing, I love how Hans grows on you like a mold, I love how naive and hopeful and just young Henry is, there’s so many gruff jaded protagonists that having him freak out at the mention of the devil or just blindly believe random sh*t or just refuse to compromise on his morals is so endearing to me. I love the world and systems for stealth and stealing and character schedules, just a pleasure to be in and play around with. But by far my favorite part of the game are the side quests, they’re so unique and fun, the rewards are universally bad but it genuinely doesn’t matter, you just go somewhere and you watch some weird, funny or creepy medieval drama unfold, and it’s different and interesting every time. I also love how your different character stats can also play into it New Vegas style.

I loved how small things in this game had a level of challenge to them.  You have to watch your characters hunger, and at the beginning of the game it's a bit hard to find food without stealing. Your equipment wears down (especially boots), and your character can stink if you don't visit the bathhouse.  I laughed when an enemy found me while I was crouching behind them just because they could smell how bad my character stunk. I also really enjoyed learning about medieval Europe as a lot of it is historically accurate with an in-depth codex’s detailing events, real noblemen, and general things like historical professions and the like. I could never in a million years have imagined that a game this hardcore and slow paced could have as few rough edges as KCD2.

The fact that myself, and seemingly most of the people that are still talking about it online drop 40-60 hours into the game before starting the first real main mission is testament to how well designed, integrated and engaging all of the systems in the game are, which for a game with such a large amount of very in depth systems is a straight up masterstroke of game design. I've played countless open world RPGs and no game has come close to getting me this deeply invested via its gameplay systems alone. Just existing as Henry, building up his stats and gear while also improving my own understanding of the game and combat evokes a feeling I can only compare to the "one more turn" feeling you get from the Civilization games. There is always something to do and a reason for me to want to do it and that feeling seemingly just never stops.

It's a lot like RDR2 for masochists and if Arthur was 15 again. It's not a "fun every minute" kind of game. It's immersive and challenging, and there's a great satisfaction loop as you improve at various things. I think it requires a bit more nuance and preparation than a lot of modern day RPGs, which can be frustrating to people expecting more of a Ghost of Tsushima type game, or a game with fights every 5 minutes. Let's say that where in RDR2 the immersion stuff felt rapidly like a chore here is linked to actual gameplay mechanics and not just for the sake of it. Personally, I think KCD2 does a great job of rewarding the extra effort that it asks of the player.

It's one of those games where the positives far outweigh the negatives. The game can be quite buggy especially in the second map, the story drags on in certain parts (especially those extended sections where you can't explore freely until you complete the quest), pacing is inconsistent, good loot is easy to obtain early game, etc. However, the writing, characters, voice acting, visuals, soundtrack, realism and detail this game has far compensate those issues. In a way it reminds me of The Witcher 3 10 years ago. I put about 100 hours into the game and don't regret a single minute of it. I'm looking forward to a second playthrough in the future, trying different choices and gameplay styles. It's GOTY contender for sure, though Clair Obscur has a strong case to win as well.

I have not felt like this about a video game since crawling out of the prison in Bethesda's Oblivion and discovering a sprawling world rife with adventure and nature. This game is not for everyone, the combat takes patience and finesse, it is a survival sim and you are not the chosen one and you will fail at conversations constantly, but this is a game for me and I'm so thrilled to have played it. I know I'm rambling here but the best comparison to make my point is Larian Studios: Divinity Original Sin 1&2 are some of the best games made for CRPG fans. Baldurs Gate 3 however is a game that creates CRPG fans. Similarly KCD1 was a very good game made for a specific niche of hardcore immersive RPGs. KCD2 I think has the potential to create fans of such games, in a way that I don't think we've seen since Skyrim.

In conclusion, I've never felt more immersed in the Middle Ages. The graphics are stunning, and the level of detail is astonishing. Everything just feels right. Even walking through the forest is so immersive it's breathtaking. This level of detail, combined with the vast possibilities the game offers, makes it an experience you don't want to miss out on! If you’re willing to sit down, take things slow, and just get lost in it, there really is no game that does it better in my opinion. I can wholeheartedly say that if you want to experience an amazing campaign set in a perfectly recreated version of life in 1403 Europe, give it a try you won't regret it.

I remember booting up KCD2 expecting a bigger, prettier version of the first game. What I got was something that pulled me in and did not let go. One moment I am riding through the countryside just to see what is over the next hill, and the next I am three hours deep into a side quest I never planned on starting. It has that same soul the first game had, just polished to a point I did not think was possible. Bohemia in KCD2 does not feel like a game map. It feels like a place. The villages have their own rhythm, the forests feel like you could actually get lost in them, and Kuttenberg is easily one of the most impressive cities I have walked through in an RPG. Henry's story grabs you early and it never really lets go, and the way KCD2 treats Czech history gives the whole thing a weight most games do not even attempt. What surprised me most was how much the small things added up. Just riding back to camp after a long day, with nothing but the music playing, ended up being one of my favorite parts of the game, and that music never once felt like background noise. Combat still has that same bite from the first game, but it is smoother now, easier to pick up if you want to keep things simple, or deep enough to master if you want real combos. Side activities like alchemy and blacksmithing pulled me in more than I expected too. 

KCD2 is not perfect. NPCs sometimes forget something happened right after a quest ends, the pacing dips depending on how you play, and Mutt got nerfed, which still stings a little. None of that changed how much I enjoyed the ride though.

As for the DLCs, the first one brings in a mysterious painter character and a string of fetch quests with a surprisingly dark undertone, and it fits nicely into the main story if you run them side by side. The second is more of a quality of life add-on. You finally get a home base with your own customizable forge to craft and rest at, though the quests tied to it can feel a bit repetitive after a while. The third DLC leans into a monastery based stealth and investigation, with strong characters, great cinematics, and a story that is decent on its own but really shines through the atmosphere. It is shorter than the others, but it is put together really well.

Finishing Kingdom Come: Deliverance II did not feel like closing out a sequel, it felt like picking up right where the first journey left off and finishing it properly. Without exaggeration, KCD and KCD2 together make up the best RPG series I have ever played. Overall, KCD2 gets a 10/10, easy recommend.

Earlier in 2025, I finished KCD1 and found myself enamoured by the game's dedication to put you in Henry's shoes, the level of immersion, details that actually affect the gameplay, the fair amount of freedom of choice and of course the clunky combat. All of which that helps culminate the KCD experience. 
So I was genuinely excited for the sequel the way everyone hyped it up to be a clear improvement from the first game. And while it isn't a huge departure, the improvements are worthy of every praise. 
These past 140 hours have probably been some of the most fun I've ever had playing any game. 

My biggest fear was that, since KCD2 is much larger, they would dumb down core mechanics for "quality of life" or to appeal to a broader audience. I’m glad they didn’t, for the most part. While there are some much needed QoL upgrades, it still feels like Kingdom Come, just more expanded and refined.


Just like the previous game, this one also takes place in Bohemian countryside and wilderness. Where the first game took more photorealistic approach with the graphics and vistas, KCD2, though still being photorealistic, has more colorful, painting-esque visuals. I really appreciate this direction, since so much medieval media is obsessed with trying to look "gritty" all the time.


Dividing the game into two regions was, in my opinion, a great decision. It keeps the first region from feeling overwhelming while giving you enough time to complete quests and prepare for what’s ahead. One of the coolest moments is when you feel like you've experienced the peak of the game, only to get hit with the, much bigger, denser, second region. And then there's also the massive living, breathing city with unique npcs, vendors with life cycle or their own and random events. It's easily one of the most impressive cities in any game.

Talking about the world, I can't forget the npcs, your attire and reputation still affect your charisma and how npcs treat you, just like the first game. But now, they are much more dynamic mixed with the in-depth crime system. You can get punished accordingly or if you have high enough charisma or speech, you might get away with it. The persuasion system is more interesting than ever now with few more options, so passing and failing them can result in different outcomes which are always fun to see play out. Reputation also plays a big part who you're talking to and now some NPCs have they're own individual reputation meters. 

On the topic of speech checks, perk system is much better integrated in the dialogues this time. For example if I have high scholarship, I can choose the dialogue that rely on it, letting me argue better with an educated npc and so on.


One of the biggest highlights of this game is the way you can meet alot of characters through pure exploration, only to meet them again in important quests. Where they'll often refer to earlier events which just adds to the immersion of making the world feel lived in. Or some minor npc that you helped long time ago will run into you and thank you. There are lots of moments like this and it really feels fulfilling to see your efforts gets recognised. 

Most of my playtime was me doing side quests and thankfully a very good amount of them were much better this time around. Alot of them had choices that reward out of the box thinking and different outcomes which lead to different side quests. So the whole thing feels like a side story rather than running errands for npcs. It also helped that a lot of them had cutscenes and good voice acting on the same quality as the main quest.

Side activities were also alot better now, often having their own quests that make them feel personalized rather than just grinding for rewards. The best example is the sword fighting tournament and how we go through a whole quest to set it up with some beloved npcs. Then of course there's the whole blacksmithing business which is a really great addition that just enhances the game's life-sim experience. Which also has a great quest with it that strengthens Henry's character.

KCD2's story is one of my favourite in gaming. Many of the themes that were established in the previous game are carried over and expanded upon in this sequel which I really like. The pacing never breaks, even at the slower missions, you always feel like you're going somewhere. The story being great is also a result of how masterfully some missions were made with hundred ways to approach them. There are big twists you can easily discover if you explore enough and the game rewards you for it. While some missions are a bit on the on the rails, they're never bad. The final stretch was a genuine masterpiece.

For the characters, Hans, Godwin are here. Who were easily my favourite in the first game, now joined with the colorful ensemble of characters that enhance the experience. There's also a gang dynamic in the story which makes Henry feel like everyone's equal compared to the first game where he was just an underling. There's simply way too many people you care about in this game that fixes my issues with the first one. 

The returning antagonists were also done really well, now showing more human sides compared to the first game where I didn't really care about them. Whenever they were on the screen, especially with Henry, you know it's going to cinema.

As a protagonist Henry is now alot better this time around. He has more agency and there's a fair amount of choice in the main and side quests with consequences that help shape his morality like you want. There were some choices that had me think for a bit before acting, all of them are enhanced by the wide range of characters we have and the dynamics they share with Henry that makes him better as a character.  

All of these story related stuff wouldn't be as good if the VA, mocap and cinematics weren't as phenomenal as they were. Everyone in the main cast went all out and the cinematics were so good it was hard to believe they're all made in-engine. Easily the some of the best cinematography I've seen in any game. There's also the soundtrack that consists of LOTR inspired themes, whimsical tavern music to accompany you on travels or a Mozart piece, Jan Valta did an amazing job.

Issues

About some issues, combat is much more streamlined this time, which is a double edged sword. There's 4 sides to attack from compared to 5 of the first game, so the combos are much simpler(it doesn't matter bc you're just gonna spam master strike anyways). But just like the first game it's easy exploit it by learning master strike and getting stronger very early. So it becomes pretty brain dead. Crowd control is much better here but still kinda flawed.

Some combat perks are genuinely very broken that you pretty much become invincible.
On the topic of perks, it's pretty easy to just max out on everything so you are an all rounder by the end of the game.

The new additions which were the crossbows and guns were also very situational, one takes half a minute to reload and the other has half the accuracy (I know, realism). So I got stuck with bows and longsword, which are very busted btw. Balancing is basically broken after some point into the game.

Another thing is there isn't much to spend your in game money on. After doing the main quest for a bit you can just have about everything you need for the rest of the game without spending much money. The two unique swords and one armor set I had were from the forge dlc.

After having played the first [i]Kingdom Come: Deliverance[/i], my expectations were high for the second iteration.

My expectations were not met, they were shattered. The sheer amount of stuff to do, the gorgeous landscape and the detail that went into creating this medieval masterpiece are just incredible. It improved on about everything from the first game, and it feels like a labour of love.

Keep in mind, I am playing hardcore mode, which means - amongst other things - no compass, no map marker of your current location and no fast travel. It makes you pay more attention to your surroundings, and you end up navigating via landmarks. I also make it a point NOT to run / gallop all the time, as I want to immerse myself into the universe created by Warhorse Studios. And yes, it is an entire universe.

The research done and all the info found in the codex really give you a good impression of medieval Bohemia. When they took some liberties for the sake of the game, they will actually mention that in the codex entries along with the reasoning. I love that meticulous approach to designing a world inhabited by NPCs who - mostly - will react in a manner you might expect. More so than in the first iteration.

Then again, this also falls short on a few occasions. For example, when I ride on an old mare, just about every NPC I come across feels it is their duty to inform me that they would never be seen dead on a shabby horse like that. Keep in mind, most are peasants who couldn't dream of ever owning a horse. And after 10 minutes of being shunned by people this gets on your nerves. And it certainly doesn't feel immersive. Same goes for all sorts of interactions initiated by NPCs in order to make the world feel more "engaging". This is an issue with nearly every single open world game. And one I think they could have improved by simply realising that a lot of times you will pass people without them feeling the need to comment on your lovely dog, your shabby old horse or the fact that your clothes are slightly dirty.

The fact that this irks me so much is less an indicator of the actual nuisance of this particular little annoyance. It rather shows how little I have to complain about so far in this game. Yes, I would like the tasks to be less "gamey" and more real-life like, but I assume that 90% of gamers would hate to do mundane stuff and rather have their adventures, regardless of whether they are super immersive or not. And I have no intention to die on that particular hill, as I still like doing some of these tasks and I have the option to ignore the rest (which I do on some occasions).

So, the fact that I am nitpicking at tiny stuff should give you a good idea about how much I actually love this game.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one of those rare sequels that makes the original feel like a proof of concept. You can tell Warhorse had a much bigger budget this time around because they took everything that worked in the first game, refined it, polished it, and somehow managed to make it all come together almost perfectly.

The biggest difference for me is just how smooth the game feels to play. I enjoyed the first game, but there was always a layer of jank sitting on top of everything. Here, almost every mechanic feels refined and far more intuitive. The movement, combat, exploration, conversations, progression, it all flows so much better than before.

What really elevates the game though is the immersion. This is genuinely one of the most immersive games I've ever played. The world feels alive in a way very few RPGs manage. NPCs follow believable daily routines, the day and night cycle affects how people behave, and everything feels grounded enough that you start treating the world like a real place rather than a video game map. One of my favourite memories was passing time blacksmithing weapons and horseshoes under shelter while it was pouring rain both in the game and in real life as well. Moments like that completely pulled me into the experience.

Kuttenberg is also one of the most impressive cities I've ever seen in a video game. The sense of scale is incredible, and walking through it genuinely feels like exploring a real medieval city. Even outside the city, the smaller villages are packed with personality and are fun to wander through. The forests deserve special mention too. This might genuinely have the best vegetation I've seen in a game. Walking through the woods, hearing the wind, birds, distant wildlife, and all the environmental sounds creates an atmosphere that's hard to describe unless you've experienced it yourself.

The story is fantastic as well. Both the main quest and side content are consistently well written, and I loved how often the game plays around with morality. So many quests avoid obvious good and bad choices, forcing you to think about what the "right" decision actually is. Henry continues to be a great protagonist, and after spending so much time with him and the supporting cast, I became genuinely attached to these characters.

I spent over 90 hours in this game and still have content left to do along with the DLC. Somehow those 90 hours absolutely flew by. Looking back, it's only when you start remembering everything you've done, every place you've visited, every character you've met, and every story you've experienced that you realise just how massive the journey actually was. This is one of the best RPGs I've ever played and an absolute must-play for anyone who loves the genre.

How do I begin?

KCD2 is a very refreshing AA game for the longest time in the midst of AI, remaster, and gameplay replayability. It has been nominated and won several awards in 2025, and now I can see it why. Like most people, I'm one of those who feel playing game nowadays seems like a chore or doesn't feel fun anymore because as a "GaMer" (*hur-dur sarcastically*), I always think how I want to win it ASAP or if I already have the prerequisite knowledge of similar games. Initially, I went blind into KCD2 while avoiding spoilers because I already played KCD in the past....and I'm glad because I feel something that I haven't felt for a long time...I'm actually having fun in single player game. I actually DESIRED it to play more, and that's not an easy exaggeration.

KCD2 is an open-world first-person RPG medieval game where you play as Henry, a friend and squire of Sir Hans Capon. The game sets heavily in historical timeline of Late Middle Ages of 1403 in Bohemia with succession war looming across the Holy Roman Empire. Your role might seem insignificant at first, but you actually play parts in the bigger picture.

Positives:
+ Very good optimization: Warhorse Studio optimization has come a long way since first KCD. I gotta say, at launch, first KCD was not the most optimized version. Even after I played it again somewhere this year, it's still not as optimized as KCD2. But KCD2 actually surprised me with 100-150 fps in Ultra 2K with FSR. There were stutters if you went into some heavily guarded areas if you are running too fast, but it's quite mild. With my PC specs, I never went under 100 fps, so the result might be varied.

+ Great story-writing and easter eggs: you will laugh, you will feel joy, you will question "what if?", you will feel sadness/empathy, but the outcome will be decided by...some dice roll. Yes, that's true. some conversation actually strike by dice rolls similar to DnD. Not too many which feels random, but it's there. Dialogue mechanic options aside, the writing in this game is...very good. Again, it's an RPG game, therefore there are some limitation with to what-if dialogues by the dev, but they basically give Henry options to be an absolute menace or good boi. Sometimes trollish even. And for modern audience, the dev understood perfectly when they put hilarious meme references you saw in internet. Very cultured indeed.

+ Gameplay mechanic and contents: since you could say KCD2 is a game which is quite close to medieval realism, it doesn't need to be as close as historical as possible. But they did. Which feels more fun and less of a medieval history simulator. That doesn't mean the content is not authentic, it's just presented as simplified history version. What I mean is, you must remember this is a GAME and not historical simulator, it doesn't have to be perfect, but at least tolerable to some degree of realism. With that put aside, the content in the game were beautifully designed than I expected and it's hard to mention it without spoiling some story or content.

You want to save your game? Too bad you need to brew a Schnapp for it. You want to buy something? Too bad you are branded now because of your past misdeed. Did you get food poisoning? Better have antidote or you will die in the next 5 minutes (accurate irl too). Ohh, you better check that grave, might be have some quest item for later. Sometimes some quest puzzle like a riddle need an ACTUAL BRAIN to solve it out. Yes, it was that detail. And I love how Warhorse gave insightful Codex to player who are interested in this periodical of time. It's like you are learning and playing at the same time (watching Ubisoft games with face palm). Like depicting NPC's daily life in medieval time of what not and what does. From the architecture of Trotsky castle to Kuttenberg city and (arguably) accurate armor and clothes in the 15th century. There will be lot of historians who will debate this, but still, kudos to Warhorse studios team for putting tremendous effort in the game for the sake of authenticity. 

In short, yes there're lot of contents in the game and justify the price tag.

+ - Good music and sound effect: I don't have lot to say. The music in the game fits perfectly on every action sequence. For example, if you are on the road, you will hear the standard lute and pandeiro so Henry won't be so lonely. Or if you are in Italian quarter, you will hear funny Italian pizza medieval music. For most part, the game will give you sequence of music based on the cinematic, location, and your action in the game. Overall, very good choice of music. That said, the SFX might need some variations. Because most of the SFX sound so high or doesn't have lot of grumble or "thump" variation except the horse hoof gallop. It's not bad per se and certainly won't affect your gameplay, but it's there.

Negatives:
- Minor bugs and soft lock: unfortunately even though I have been such a fanboy about this game, it's with heavy heart that I also must come clean that this game is not without bugs. No game is perfect, and KDC2 is one of those. For example, Kuttenberg Tournament quest notification have such infamous bug where you need to return the gears but it won't allow you, therefore you could just leave the tournament or pay the gear to remove the notification. It's a minor bug I say, but it's annoying because it's such a wake up call. Another example is an investigation quest in Forge DLC where you need to investigate lost materials or schematic for the guild. If you "accidentally" learned one of the required schematic, it will count as lost item and you couldn't lie nor decline the quest to fail it. So the notification dangling there awkwardly and you can't finish the quest. Or maybe you met with strangers in Kuttenberg street, but you couldn't see who you are talking to because they already gone behind the cart in marketplace. For completionist, you better make some Schnapp in case you soft lock some choices (or maybe that's part of the gameplay?).

- Limited save slot: this is just me being very picky. Like aforementioned above, I need to save a lot because I want to try to finish all the side quest first, then the main quest. Therefore I need to save a lot. Turn out, you only could have 500 slots or you need to overwrite the older saves.

- Questionable decent-ish stealth mechanic: this is more like a complaint. Since it's very weird that sometimes enemy could have x-ray vision to see the body inside the building or night vision which could see a body from far away even though it's so damn dark unless you need to get close to it. It's not bad, but it's not good either.

And that's probably it. Kudos to TomMckay (Henry VA), rest of the casts, professional sources, and the developers, you all did brilliantly. Go give KCD2 a try. It's worth the full price, and even better on discount.

This is my first ever public review of a game, and for a damned good reason. I will address both KCD1 and 2, because you’re mistaken if you think you can fully enjoy the second game without playing the first. 

Earlier this year, I played KCD1 at the behest of my friend. It was unpalatable to me. The combat was clunky, the graphics were dated, and the overall gameplay was otherwise cumbersome and difficult. The map, its large swath of characters, the various choices I could make – it all felt too big and overwhelming. 

I never thought I'd fall so deeply in love with it. I thugged out the initial discomfort, and before I could say "[i]are you yanking my pizzle?[/i]", I was burning an egregious amount of midnight oil toiling away at side quests, sharpening my skills, and immersing myself in the breathtaking world of 15th century Bohemia. As a history nerd, KCD scratched an decades-old itch in my brain that was last tended to when I played Assassin's Creed 2 as a kid. Its deep realism doesn't just start with its historical storyline, though. KCD features a challenging uphill climb where you grow from a naive peasant boy to a skilled and noble warrior. It doesn't hold your hand, and refuses to mollycoddle you under the pretext that you're the protagonist. It is precisely this unforgiving aspect that earned this franchise my deep and profound respect. 

If KCD1 is an [i]antipasto[/i], KCD2 is the [i]primo[/i], [i]secondo[/i], and [i]dolce[/i] all wrapped up in a platter of seamless gameplay, engaging storylines, clever humour, BAFTA-worthy voice acting, and environments so alive and detailed that you can almost smell the tavern mildew through the screen. The beauty and diversity of KCD2’s world frequently compelled me to slow down and watch the sun setting from the hills, saunter through the woods, or sit inside a chapel for a moment of repose amidst the swashbuckling, gritty realism of medieval wartime. Through its many, [i]many[/i] quests and NPCs that feel like real, relatable people, KCD2 commands a level of immersion and realism unparalleled to any RPG game. 

KCD’s combat is demanding, to say the least. Reminiscent of [i]For Honor[/i]’s combat system, KCD practically screams medieval immersion. With combos, parries, and feints running alongside a ridiculous amount of gear and weapons at your disposal, you’ll spend what seems like a frustrating (and oftentimes embarrassing) amount of time trying to take down a couple of lightly-armoured bandits. It’s for this reason that it feels so exceptionally rewarding. KCD2 does simplify the combat system from its predecessor, but does so without sacrificing the fundamentals that made it so great in the first place.

I could ramble on and on, but I think I’ve made my point. KCD swallows the RPG genre and spits out its best qualities in spades. I’ve dedicated over 200 hours of my life to this franchise, and I still find myself hungry for more. Jesus Christ be praised, and may the Lord watch over Warhorse Studios for creating such a masterpiece.

Your rep and appearance changes how NPC's treat you; when you're the outsider you're treated like one (eg: the first person they blame for any crime) but when you have a good rep some speech skills and the right outfit you can get away with murder but be warned crime has consequences such as fines, jail time, whipping with no safeword, branding and even death. Rep makes a huge difference for example try walking around a town with your weapon out with a low rep and guards will immediately approach you and tell you to put it away and if you ignore them they will attempt to arrest you and shove you in the stocks but if you have a good rep in the same town guards will tell you to put it away but won't chase you and just go about their shift because they know and trust you. All the miners have scouser accents to represent the cultural divide between them and the rest of society (Bohemian's didn't go to Liverpool and kidnap a bunch of them). Story and side quest actions and dialogue have some consequences, there's some character development that made me question who is good or evil and I don't mean a blue Marvel villain, it's deeper than that, I even found myself giving a Toth about the fate of some of them. There's some optional romances for Henry in there too, you can even take Henry and Capon's bromance to the next level (with a different kind of swordplay) or easily avoid that without being mean or affecting the plot, it's all very clear (and doesn't feel "woke" or like pandering, if anything it's the devs throwing a bone to the fan art that came out of the first game). The plot can be serious, heartfelt and tragic at times but it has a nice balance as there's also some funny moments too such as getting drunk, a Muslim claiming they treat women with greater respect, Henry's excuses for committing crimes and more. It's not perfect of course but there's no such thing. It takes a large chunk of poetic license for obvious narrative reasons it also tries to be historically accurate too such as the weapons and armour of the time, historical events and characters, a slimy Frenchman who's talk is far greater than his actual deeds and everyone (regardless of culture) having a huge drinking problem and btw alcoholism can be a very useful tool if used correctly.

The developers unfortunately used AI translation rather than humans so bare that in mind if you're against the replacement of human beings but you're getting plenty of human-made content for your groschen here and it's clearly a beautifully crafted game made with passion but this game is not for the instant gratification generation. It's a medieval life simulator. What you need to ask yourself is: Are you okay with hardcore roleplaying? Do you mind taking care of your gear, sharpening your weapons, washing yourself and eating food regularly, carrying a lot of sacks? Are you okay spending time making stuff rather than a simple click? Are you prepared to level up both Henry (to make stuff like lockpicking easier) and level up yourself (to get the hang of some systems and combat) Do you like a bit of medieval history? I'd been sticking to the non-combat stuff because after a few very bad combat experiences I thought I must have been undergeared, after training up my skills and getting some adequate gear and a bit of sparring in I tried again, but still ran into major difficulties.  Later found there's a target lock-on system and a controller has a much easier time with the quick directional inputs needed for the ultimate combat technique, an ability called master strike, basically a perfectly timed directional parry that counters an enemy for big damage.

I felt a bit more confident in combat for a time, until unnamed forest bandits started using master strikes against me.  From then on I stuck mostly to melee grapples and master strikes, there's a whole system of combo attacks for all the different weapons you can find, but the problem with any enemy able to pick up a sword being capable of hard countering any attack you can do and often one-shotting you leads you to feeling forced into playing a defensive game of master strikes, just so the enemy doesn't master strike you! After a bit of investigation it seemed a lot of people felt the same way, and modding out master strikes looks very popular.

That was the biggest downside I found to the game, the world is gorgeous and interesting to explore, systems of wear and dirt and blood have you cleaning up your appearance to boost your charisma before talking to others, or you might want to keep some dirt on if you're going thieving at night, there's even a talent to make you stealthier when you're dirtier.

Oh I should mention the save system, I absolutely appreciate the intention here to prevent savescumming by tying saving to a consumable item, resting or exiting the game, however in practice it means a cautious player like myself ends up spending a lot of time harvesting herbs and crafting save game consumables to the point that it feels a bit too grindy for my taste.  Fortunately one of the most popular mods available adds a quicksave, while this does go against the intention of the developers, losing hours of gameplay because of stupid human mistakes felt a bit too punitive for me. Kingdom Come: Deliverance is a rare example of an RPG based on medieval historical events that doesn't make you want to stick two fingers down your throat and lose your lunch. And while it takes plenty of liberties with history, the game still brilliantly captures the spirit of the era and manages to tell a far-from-boring story about a certain bastard.

Let me state right off the bat that I do not recommend playing the second part until you have finished the first. Franchise games are usually designed so that a player can jump in at any point and fully enjoy the experience, but that is not the case here. Even with the inclusion of flashbacks, there is still a wealth of information that requires having played the first game. That isn't a bad thing, though it is a relatively risky move for a big-budget project. Fortunately, the risk paid off.

Compared to the first game, the combat system has been slightly simplified. Henry can now wield early gunpowder pistols, crossbows, and polearms. While the gunpowder weapons and crossbows are fun to use, I can't say anything good about the polearms.

As for the main storyline, it is every bit as good as the first game's. There is still plenty of room for tense moments and drama, as well as a touch of comedy. The finale is particularly intense, though I do have reservations about the narrative's moral stance. Let’s just say I don’t quite subscribe to the philosophy that Henry should always turn the other cheek whenever possible. The game tries to teach that revenge is always wrong, yet the issue of impunity is never addressed. But that is the developer’s worldview — their message. There is nothing to be done about that.

You’ll find a handful of interesting stories among the side quests. Most of them didn't really stick in my memory, though. There are a great many tedious "fetch-and-carry" tasks that serve only as a means of earning money — honestly (or close enough to it). Speaking of the economy, getting rich in the game isn't particularly difficult, provided you don't mind looting fallen enemies and selling off the gear. Your main obstacle is simply the limited amount of Groschen in the merchants' purses.

As for the DLC content, I was largely disappointed. I can only praise *Mysteria Ecclesiae* for unlocking a new location and offering a reasonably interesting storyline. *Legacy of the Forge* failed to impress me due to its guild reputation system; I simply had no desire to grind just to complete a mini-storyline, especially since the opening setup made the ending all too predictable. As for *Brushes with Death*, it struck me as the most tedious and awful DLC of the lot. Instead of a mysterious artist, you get an annoying, schizophrenic whiner who constantly demands you complete the most boring tasks imaginable. His personal story is simply uninteresting. The remaining DLCs offer no narrative content — only gear that makes the early game significantly easier — so I chose not to use them.

I highly recommend the game, if only for its main storyline. It is superb — as are the antagonists and allies Henry encounters along the way. Clearly, the developers left room for the franchise to continue. I look forward to the third part of the story.

KCD1 was a fantastic game with its incredible story, gameplay, visuals and immersion and KCD2 is whatever is better than all that.

I feel like I should start out by saying that I have seen a lot of people ask if they should complete the first game first or if they can just jump directly into KCD2, and I would highly recommend completing the first game first. It is important to understand the story and that you have developed a bond with the recurring characters in the world. The story in this game is just as important as everything else.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story in KCD2 takes off right after the end of KCD1, after ending the siege on Talmberg Castle, rescuing Sir Radzig and Lady Stephanie and witnessing Istvan Toth's peaceful escape. Henry and Hans Capon are sent to the Trosky region of Bohemia on a diplomatic mission to find further support and allies for the imprisoned King Wenceslas IV and this is where KCD2 takes off. Right after the opening scene, Henry and Hans Capon's party enters the Trosky region, meeting Captain Thomas and his party. They warn them of a dangerous bandit group who has been terrorizing the land. I won't say anything more about the actual story to avoid spoiling anything. Just know that it is great and a big part of why this game is so good.

[h3]Combat[/h3]
I know there is a mixed opinion on whether or not the combat in KCD2 is better or not than in KCD1 and while I do agree that it is more nuanced, less abusable and maybe more realistic, it does have issues that the combat in KCD1 didn't have.

They changed how combat works in KCD2 and it did throw me off a bit at the start. The big problem with it is that there is no good way to train combat early on. Yes, you can duel Tomcat, but it isn't a repeatable tutorial that teaches you blocking and how you keep distance and it is only just him, what you really need to train early on is how to beat multiple opponents outnumbering you. This makes combat quite unpleasant for the first many hours of this game. I guess the best advice I can give is to be patient, most of the time I died in combat it was because of bad stamina management, being too aggressive and not keeping distance. Footwork is actually very important in KCD2 combat, especially when you are alone against multiple opponents. It is very important to learn how to move around so that they do not encircle you and hit you from all sides, you want them always to be in front of you. So, I would train that first if you are struggling. However, it is also important to know, that you are very weak in early game KCD1 and you will encounter a lot of enemies you aren't necessarily supposed to beat, so it is totally okay to just run away.

If you want some video tutorials, I did find these two videos helpful: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=en277l3o2KU https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EvtRNCERZmY

Where this combat system has taken a hit in my opinion is with masterstrikes and overpowered swords. The developers really want you to play with your father's longsword in this game and therefore they made it so that masterstrikes are only possible while wielding a sword. This really sucks, if you like me don't like swords much. My preferred weapon throughout both games was the warhammer and in KCD2, while it is still very strong, it can be really hard to dodge sword wielding enemies, you will pretty much have to rely on dodging instead, but even that has its issues, especially when facing more than one opponent.

Out of the swords, the two handed swords are definitely the most overpowered. From my experience, the two handed sword opponents were by far the scariest. They block better than any shielded opponent, they all masterstrike almost perfectly, they hit really hard and they often also block strikes after dodges. I can't count how many times I got knocked out after only 2 - 3 strikes from a two handed sword while wearing some of the best heavy armor in the game. It also doesn't make any sense why so many opponents wield two handed swords when it wasn't a particularly good weapon and therefore not a commonly used one in the Middle Ages. They were more of a status symbol rather than a good weapon. We should really see more polearms and maces than swords around.

But two handed swords aren't the only issue combat in KCD2 has. Fist fights are utterly broken. It doesn't matter how much steel your fists are covered in and how many deadly blows you deal to your unarmored opponent's face, if the game considers him high level and skilled, fist fights can go on for minutes with your opponent showing no signs of loss of fatigue or injury. It is funny that fist fights are made this badly when they throw you into fist fights a lot throughout this story.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Beside combat, the rest of the gameplay is very similar to KCD1, sometimes maybe a bit too similar. Mission directives are still as bad as they were in KCD1 and it really makes no sense, since it isn't like they tried to go overly hardcore on the realism to where you have to always find your own way, because they will still show you on the map where to go. There is just a lot of missing and hard to read markers and badly worded descriptions in the quest log that sometimes makes it really hard to understand what to do, it is just badly designed.

What I do really like though, is that this game has a lot of different quests with choices that really matter on the outcome of the world and Henry's story. You are actually given choices in this game through dialogue that might not seem like much at first, but then it turns out that if you had been more careful with your words or kept certain things to yourself, it might have saved entire villages worth of civilian lives, and I really like that.

Another great change is that the AI is now a lot smarter and way more careful with you sneaking around and entering their property. They can hear and spot you from pretty far away and if they see you sneaking around, they will check if you stole anything and report your behavior. This goes hand in hand with the reputation system in all the cities where you can see how well liked or hated you are.

I will say though, it is a major oversight not to have added a preview for your horse when shopping for horse equipment. It was so annoying having to make a save every time I wanted to shop for horse cosmetics.

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The first game was impressive for its time and still looks good today a decade later, but this second game isn't just impressive visually, it is truly breathtaking at times. The attention to detail in the environmental design is really admirable and sometimes when there is no one around and the light is just perfect, the scenery can almost look like a real picture.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
Even if it isn't perfect, this is still one of the best games I have ever played and I have it ranked 6 on my top 100. It has a high learning curve, but it is so worth the time you invest into learning it.

Open worlds nowadays are something that actually scares a gamer like me away. You know - all those points of interest, outposts, and often pointless exploration that gives you nothing but the feeling that you just wasted your time. Well... I can say that this world sucked me in for about 90 hours before I realized I no longer wanted to explore it, having completed most of the content and then focusing specifically on the remaining main story.

Compared to the first game, KCD2 is much more player-friendly. Throwing Henry into a village where it is simply easier to start was definitely the right decision. In the first game it took me about 10 hours to settle in and understand how to actually play [i](after which KCD2 was announced and I dropped the first game)[/i], while here it took me only around 5 hours after the prologue. The game's meticulous mechanics initially scared me off - where after a real-life workday you basically do another job inside the game: forging swords, brewing potions, doing routine tasks. But in practice everything turned out to be much more engaging than expected. Some clunkiness and slowness are still there and do stretch the playtime [i](for example, the lack of auto-brewing)[/i], yet at the same time they undeniably enhance immersion. Once you start treating it as part of the gameplay loop, the game fully pulls you in.

It was a rare case where at the beginning, out of pure ignorance, I searched for videos not about quest walkthroughs, but about how to even start playing the game properly. I admit - I have become a bit too casual as a player these days. I spent around 40 hours in the starting area, either enjoying or suffering through the local rules and life simulation. At some point I got used to it and even started enjoying it. Probably because the level of detail and immersion is so high that it simply does not get boring - at least not too quickly. I would say the game strikes a very well-balanced mix of medieval simulation and gameplay, where routine itself becomes a core mechanic.

Around the 40-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade.

After the mid-game, interest in exploration unfortunately starts to decline [i](especially if you complete all side quests before unlocking a new region)[/i], because there is no longer a real need to clear everything, and you become so experienced that the challenge decreases. Those tense moments - like trying to perfectly handle three opponents at once or cracking a valuable lock - become rarer, and those were some of the most memorable parts for me. Eventually you move from petty thievery in villages to infiltrating castles and estates. Still, even with the best equipment you can absolutely get wrecked by bandits, so player skill and experience still matter a lot.

Around the 70-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade.

I was honestly surprised to see that the game still runs on CryEngine, because visually it can easily rival what once was the technological benchmark - Crysis. Lush green forests, excellent sound design [i](although some tracks do become repetitive if you stay in the world for too long)[/i], beautiful lighting - especially in HDR mode. The work of the artists and designers deserves special applause: you can easily get lost just admiring the scenery and architecture. This will be particularly enjoyable for players interested in medieval history. For those who want to dive deeper, there is an in-game codex and even a very entertaining official YouTube channel. The life simulation aspect, which perhaps impressed me more when I was younger, here simply works naturally and convincingly, making the world feel believable. All gameplay systems feel carefully balanced to keep the player engaged.

Around the 100-hour mark the game started to feel slightly repetitive, and the initial excitement slowly began to fade.

Overall, I would say the quests are about 50/50. Half of them are just regular tasks without anything particularly special, while the other half are genuinely memorable and interesting stories. There are many side quests, and some of them are surprisingly intricate in unexpected ways, which is a definite plus. Closer to the end, some narrative patterns start to repeat, but it is hard to complain too much about that. It can be frustrating when a quest has a hidden timer and you miss a trigger that locks certain content. Even after completing quests, some consequences can later be encountered in the world, which is a nice touch. Still, I occasionally had to check guides to avoid wasting too much time searching for solutions. The good thing is that most quests are not just "map markers" - they are actual stories: funny, sad, or dramatic. Some of them genuinely give you goosebumps.

To avoid making the game sound perfect - quest rewards often feel more symbolic than truly useful, although this depends on your playstyle. And when the game makes you travel back and forth across the map multiple times, it stops being amusing quite quickly. The infamous "bag-carrying" quests are funny the first couple of times, but by the eighth time it becomes a bit too much. The city is huge and changes the gameplay significantly, but you will spend a lot of time running through it, and fast travel points are somewhat limited, which can feel exhausting. The game's budget occasionally shows through, mostly in the reuse of character models.

And of course, the ultimate highlight of the game is its story. Everything related to the main quest and cinematic set-pieces [i](which are generally great even in many side quests)[/i] deserves nothing but praise. Acting, camera work, cutscenes - all are top-notch, and it is hard to believe this is all done within an in-game engine. The meticulous attention to detail in many scenes makes them truly memorable. This is exactly the level of immersion you expect from a large-scale RPG so it does not feel like just another disposable blockbuster. The story is both fun and heavy, and brutally medieval at times. The characters are memorable, and it feels genuinely sad when the adventure finally comes to an end - which is a clear sign of a truly great game.

P.S. I would also like to highlight the localization - the richness of the language is conveyed very well, and native speakers will likely be satisfied.
While this franchise may not be for everyone, it is easily within my top 5 of all time. From the storytelling to characters to environments to attention to detail, it truly is a masterpiece.

I actually finished this game a long time ago but never had the time to talk about it. But still, this is the best RPG of 2025 in my opinion.
The RPG vibe in this game is really strong. It reminds me a lot of Baldur’s Gate 3 where you can approach situations in many different ways and basically do whatever you want depending on how you want to handle things. But just like the first game, this isn’t a game for everyone.
There are a lot of improvements compared to the previous game, both in graphics and overall quality of life features.
Story-wise, it continues directly from Kingdom Come Deliverance 1, where the main character and his friends are tasked with delivering a letter to the lord of Trosky. A lot of people might ask if you need to play KCD1 first to understand the story of KCD2. My answer is yes and no.
If you played KCD1 before jumping into KCD2, you’ll definitely feel a sense of familiarity and connection with characters like Sir Radzig and Sir Hanush. After everything the main character goes through in KCD2, there’s this feeling of relief when those characters finally show up, like you just want to say “finally.” There are also moments where you don’t only play from the main character’s perspective, and I think that part makes more sense if you already know who that person is from the first game.
If you jump straight into KCD2, the game does give you short flashbacks explaining the story of the first game. But in my opinion, you won’t really feel attached to the returning characters, especially the important ones.

Gameplay-wise, there are a lot of important additions that really improve the experience. One of the biggest ones is the new detection system called the Behaviour Indicator with a hare icon. It helps a lot if you want to play stealth. You can see when someone is looking for you, when you’re entering restricted areas, and other useful indicators.
The combat mechanics in the sequel feel easier compared to the first game. That’s actually understandable because the story continues from KCD1 and the main character is already more experienced with combat. It only starts to feel challenging again when you try using the new weapon introduced in this game, the handgun. But still, don’t get overconfident and try fighting a big group of enemies alone.
One thing I noticed in combat is that the attack directions are simplified compared to the first game, and switching stances to choose attack directions feels much smoother now.

This sequel also has a lot of quests that are surprisingly funny, both main quests and side quests. The humor doesn’t always come from actual jokes. Sometimes it’s just the stupid things the characters do that make the situation awkward and funny at the same time.
For example, there’s a side quest where you help two musicians get a lute. There are multiple ways to solve it. You can either steal the lute or buy it. If you buy it, the musicians will arrive safely at their destination city. But if you steal the lute, both of them end up getting arrested when they reach the city, and you can find them again later being punished there.
There are also a lot of new activities added to the game. You can do horseback archery, participate in horse races where you’re free to take any route as long as you reach the checkpoints, work as a blacksmith, customize your hairstyle, mustache, and beard, and many more. With so many side quests and activities, it’s honestly hard to get bored playing this game.

Most of the downsides I found are pretty minor. For example, the romance system isn’t as deep as it was in the first game. In this sequel, romance mostly leads to a single sex scene, while in the first game you could go on multiple dates with Theresa and even give her gifts.
Another small detail is the alchemy system. In KCD1, when you added herbs into the pot, you could actually see them floating in the liquid. In KCD2, no matter what ingredient you add, you only see the color of the liquid and nothing else.
There’s also the removal of the automatic potion crafting feature. In KCD1, once you reached a certain level you could auto craft potions. In KCD2 you have to craft them manually again, although at higher levels you can produce around five or six potions at once.

But again, despite the flaws I mentioned, I had a great time playing this game for a very long time. I honestly think this game deserved to win at least one award, especially for Best RPG.

I completed my first run in around 140 hours. Kingdom Come: Deliverance II delivers an ultra massive and immersive RPG experience. The studio clearly aimed for a lot of realism, and they pulled it off pretty well. It’s crazy how many small details are included. The quests and story are well written, and the side quests (separate from activities, since they’re two different things) are interesting to do.
The crafting system is one of the best I’ve ever seen in a video game.

Combat is hard to master, and I love that you actually have to train to improve. It really helps you get more involved in the game. Once you reach a specific area, you unlock a technique (sword only) that makes fights much easier. There are plenty of weapons available, from melee to ranged, so it suits different playstyles.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a great game, but there are a few flaws…
One thing I didn’t like: imagine being 1 centimeter away from a helmetless bandit, crossbow fully charged, aiming at his head… and he doesn’t die just because you don’t have enough perks or points in ranged weapons.
Or another situation: you’re in full plate armor, meet a bandit... and he can one shot you, especially in the second area. 
Some quests can also fail just because you’re too slow. And having to re-equip ALL your gear after certain moments is annoying.
But they are nothing compared to the overall experience.

I highly recommend Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, even at full price, which honestly isn’t that high compared to other games.

Honestly, I never expected to like this game. I thought it would be "too difficult", "too realistic", and that it would take all the fun out of playing. But after finishing the first part, I realized that it’s very close to being a masterpiece. The realism is exactly where it needs to be.
So I started the second part with high expectations, and this time it’s not just “close to a masterpiece” - IT IS A MASTERPIECE!

The world feels incredibly alive and beautiful. The forests, especially, are something else - you can wander through them for hours and just enjoy the atmosphere. The voice acting and performances are great, and the story is amazing, a big step up from the first game. The biggest improvement is in the cutscenes. This is what you’d call “absolute cinema.”
The combat system is more interesting now, with a wider variety of weapons. However, there is one issue: the master strike with a longsword is still so effective that it kind of discourages you from using other weapon types like halberds or axes.

Alchemy has become more engaging, and the new blacksmithing mechanic is fantastic. I probably spent around 20 hours just forging different items. Social mechanics have also improved a lot, e.g. - random encounters during fast travel can turn into full mini-storylines that sometimes last almost until the end of the game.

If you’re hesitant because the game seems "too realistic" or "too difficult" just don’t overthink it. Give it a chance!

And finally… a fountain here in the middle of the city, where does the water come from?????
It is one of the best games of the century, and one of the best narrative-driven games. If you haven't played KCD2 yet, what are you waiting for?

I'm going to get my value out of this game, but there have been some things which are quite irksome which overall give the sense of the game being an unfinished product, and at times a nuisance to play. There are many aspects about this game I really like, but at this stage I honestly don't get the hype.

- Quite a misleading trailer: this feels like a medieval simulator more than an adventure-rpg I was expecting. This is done for realism according to the internet, but the following points completely break any realism in the game which makes it feel quite slow, lame and boring to play at times.

- Horse combat sucks. Any mounted warrior was a fearsome opponent in those times. In KCD2, charging down even a bandit feels unintuitive, and lacks all the power and fun of smashing into an unarmoured enemy I was hoping for. 

- That same bandit will have unlimited stamina to chase you on your horse, at times I've galloped down a path, turned to charge the opponent, and I don't have enough time to even fully turn before he is making a swing as he has somehow managed to keep up as a fully armed and armoured "bandit" with a galloping horse (but you swing a sword 3-4 times and you are breathless on horseback).

- On the note of bandits, it's not long into the game you will be heading down a path thinking "ah a fellow knight, good day sir" for it to turn out to be a "bandit" in full chainmail/armour. Going back to the "realism" aspect, it just feels immersion breaking to have such heavily armed and armoured opponents so early on (unless potentially this ties into the story somehow). The next section down you will see a man/woman travelling solo in full cloth. If the roads were that dangerous, not a single person would leave the villages/towns. Again, immersion breaking.

- So much filler dialogue. While it's awesome to have the game fully voice-acted, it feels like low quality dialogue. As someone that is a huge fan of following a story in many games (disco elysium, cyberpunk, elder scrolls, Baldurs Gate 3) and will quite happily sit through hours of compelling dialogue, in KCD2 it feels lacking. Uninspired quantity over quality type of deal. So much jargon and even foreign languages are thrown in that sometimes you feel you need a translator to get the context.

- Unskippable "walk/ride through the forest" scenes. Replaying this game must be so draining. Games like Skyrim you could enjoy this as the landscape was shifting and was interesting to view from different angles and kept these sequences relatively short, with a lower frequency. For KCD2 it's the bread and butter of the game: go for slow walk through repeating landscapes of thick forest, grassy meadows, more trees, more grass, pond, small pond, rocks. 

- Very grindy, I play on hardcore and you must create potions to be able to save. It seems the places you can stash your gear are nowhere near where you can craft items, which is even further away in the opposite direction to where you can sell them. You can’t carry all your items with you, yet you need different armour sets/crafting mats for say combat and/or speech. So before getting the horse early on it brought me close to tears with all the running up and down the same old paths to maybe sell 3 items or crafting a few potions. To gather the crafting mats you must press E on them 100 times. When you do craft items to sell, you will get next to nothing for them. At which point you are exhausted and hungry so you need to travel to fix that. This is all before you can set out to do the thing you wanted to do in the first place. I’m a fan of the hardcore experience, I love a good challenge and consider it my go-to in games and typically really enjoy the experience, whereas in this game they feel like frustrating slow additional labour that has no respect for your time.

- Selling items, it is unclear who will buy/sell what and to travel for 20 mins to a town who is a blacksmith that will only buy a few weapons and none of your armour you've just lugged halfway across the map is a pain. 

- Part of the "realism," will be starting a fair duel with someone where they are swinging a sword at you before the game has even fully faded from black after a load screen. Or if you started the dialogue from horseback, you are being pulled off horseback. Ive tested this by saving before hand and starting a duel, even if I'm smashing the block or attack button nothing has time to prevent this first bit of damage from being taken. You have to be immediately sprinting away. Why would these combat sequences not start a few paces away from each other with your weapon already drawn?

Features that are missing that makes the game feel like it's in beta stage and/or immersion breaking:
- Inventory management sucks. You can design “outfits” that can be utilised for various situations (e.g. speech outfit), but as soon as you store it, the game will “forget” it was part of your outfit. No ability to mark items for sale. No ability to sort-by weight to value ratio. The armour organisation is poor considering how many slots there are.
- Hardcore mode compass (that doesn’t provide cardinal directions) that can not be switched off
- No auto-run feature
- NPCs will go from thick eastern European accent to Obi-Wan "Hello there" as you pass them, or someone in pillory going from grovelling ruffian to "Ah, God grace us today, friend"
- Sound design feels lacklustre at times. Swing a huge crushing blow to head with your sword? Sounds like someone hitting a teacup with a spoon.
- A huge amount of the game mechanics are not explained in the slightest and require extra-curricular learning or forum trawling to discover. Very punishing and time consuming to get wrong.
- Combat feels jank, clearly designed for a controller. Moving the mouse to change direction of a swing only to end up looking off to the side to then get your head smashed in. The tab-targeting, quick time event, run away circle back to swing once or punch once feels lame and boring. 
- Horseback combat sucks outside of horseback archery competitions, which I really enjoyed
- Marksmanship combat is not viable in the slightest, even after being patient and levelling it. Enemies will take 2/3 crossbow bolt's to the face at point blank range before going down, and they will often kill you before you have a chance to slowly put away your ranged weapon and draw your melee weapon.
- I purchased all the expansions because they were on sale and thought why not seeing as it's rated so highly. I get to my first chest and there appears to be some of the best weapons and armour in the game already sat in my chest while I'm just about scraping up enough money to not starve to death - no way to turn this off, or hide it behind some kind of quest/progression sequence.
- The game supposedly is about choices, but so far, everything feels very inconsequential in the decision-making process. 

There are many aspects of the game I do enjoy and will update this list as I've got my teeth stuck into it a bit more.

This winter holiday I took time out of my incredibly busy schedule of playing video games for half of the the day to instead play Kingdom Come Deliverance 1 and 2 for half of the day. It was meant to be, because I love both clunky RPGs and ambitious eurojank, and I ended up enjoying the first one so much that the potential review for that game that I was floating about in my mind was instantly discarded as I wanted to play the sequel that much, and here I am now, 80 hours later. 

While I was initially somewhat worried about the simplification of the skill system and combat system, I was very pleased that the simplification actually did things for the core systems. Combos are actually finally doable instead of being something you pray to god will happen. Combat is thus basically the same but actually works all of the time instead of when Czech Catholic Jesus decides to smile upon you. The combat system is much improved, and weapons other than longswords feel very fun and good to use, but it's insanely easy to cheese with the masterstrike and you once again end up using basically nothing but a longsword. Sometimes the perk system is quite boring, the survival skill for an example will at times just give you one hunting and one herbalism skill to pick between, instead of giving me two hunting perks to choose between to give more depth. But hey, I would much rather take three steps forward one step back than whatever slop is pushed out by triple a these days.

The game is fully voiced and so is your protagonist, and as always it comes with some tradebacks. You often times only have two-three things you can tell characters and it can lead to some conversations feeling short, but on the flipside the actual voice acting is excellent so it's not a huge deal. As far as I understand this is the longest video game script in history so they tried their best, and mostly succeeded. I'm not fully convinced that RPGs should be fully voiced, but this is a game which proves what can be done with a fully voiced cast.

The writing is sharp and fun. This game could've very easily fell into the trope of making everything grimdark and having everything sucks because you're in the middle of an enemy invasion, but instead the game perfectly balances it with the good in humans. Humans are complex beings and the game knows this, every good person you meet has their flaws and every bad guy has depth, no expense is spared in drilling it into you that you're simply taking a side in a civil war. I very much enjoy how every derived stat in speech this time around got a bad version. You don't just have speech but also coercion, impression has domination as its counterpart and presence has intimidation as its counterpart. This is quite honestly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ingenious design by the devs, it gives real depth to the conversations in a way that never quite existed in the first one. 

I quite enjoyed how many different groups of Bohemian society were included in this game. The jewish community of Bohemia finally played a large role which is fitting considering how large and old it is. Due to the game taking place in larger urban settlements the game features much more Germans than the first one, both german speaking Bohemians and people from the Holy Roman Empire at large. Bohemia at this point was quite cosmopolitan and it's cool to see it reflected in the cast. A nice touch is how Moravians are always shown to speak Scottish, reflecting how they speak Czech but a much different dialect than the Bohemians you meet. 

Quest design was KCD's greatest strength and they don't disappoint me here. I don't think any quest really hit the highs of The House of God or Plague, but I do think overall the quality is close to those two across the board. The bar for quest design is permanently raised by KCD2 and that's probably the highest praise I could give to any game.

[b] Kingdom Come: Deliverance II [/b] is a game that gave me many hours of great fun and felt like a clear step forward compared to the first game.
