I finished Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2, and overall the experience was great. It’s true that the beginning was slow and a bit heavy, but as the story progressed the game developed noticeably and the experience improved a lot. The story is very well written, and the characters are engaging and convincing, which was one of the strongest elements of the game for me.

The biggest downside I faced was the combat system. Yes, you do learn skills and unlock abilities over time, but the combat style itself remains quite repetitive, mostly based on blocking and then striking. After a while it becomes somewhat boring and doesn’t offer enough variety to keep encounters fun all the time.

The realism of injuries was also sometimes exaggerated. Breaking an arm or a leg forces you to constantly use bandages and treatment, which turns from a fun realism element into something annoying that interrupts the flow of gameplay.

The inventory interface and menus are also very cluttered and not intuitively organized. There’s a lot of unnecessary elements that make the player confused when managing gear and items.

Another negative point is the limited in-game translations and the lack of official Arabic support, which makes following the story and fine details harder for many players.

Review: Kingdom Come: Deliverance II – A Beautiful, Tedious Mess

If the goal of Kingdom Come: Deliverance II was to make me feel the crushing weight of 15th-century peasant life, then it is a resounding success. However, if the goal was to provide an engaging, functional gaming experience, it stumbles into the mud and stays there.

Ambition Over Execution
Developer Warhorse Studios clearly doubled down on the "hardcore realism" that defined the first game. While the scope of Bohemia is breathtaking, the performance is abysmal. Clunky Combat and Artificial Difficulty

Henry’s movements are agonizingly sluggish, and the lock-on system is a death sentence when facing more than one opponent. Buggy Bohemia
Then there are the bugs. From quest-breaking NPC pathfinding to physics engine freak-outs that launch Henry into the stratosphere, the game feels undercooked. Final Verdict
The writing and historical authenticity are top-tier, but they are buried under a mountain of technical instability and archaic design choices. KCD2 feels like a game built for a very specific type of masochist. If you enjoy fighting the controls as much as you enjoy fighting bandits, you’ll love it. For everyone else, this is a beautiful, bloated, and deeply frustrating experience that desperately needed another six months in the oven.

If you've come for Balder's Gate style fantasy and Skyrim magic systems, you will be disappointed -- at first. But once you gain an understanding for what this game aims to be, you will be instantaneously hooked. I've played this game four times start to finish in 2025, it's release year, and I still haven't done everything yet across all four playthroughs.

If you're a history buff like me, you'll enjoy the historically accurate setting of Bohemia in the year 1403. It's a game that does very little to hold your hand; instead, it trusts YOU, the player, to set out into the world, learn and grasp the games mechanics, and understand that you are NOT "The Chosen One", the "Main Character" -- you are Henry, just a peasant, elevated to squire (from KCD1) and have an inkling more status than that of the common farmhand.

Nobody cares who you are and you wont be the One Man to Save the World. You're another nameless person who will not have a page in history, but you will witness it unfold in real time and even take part in it. 

Real life names and real life events from 1403 history are painted seamlessly into this world while you survive inside of it. Real locations that still persist to this day are fully explorable, most NPCs (and especially named ones) have a 24 hour schedule that push the immersion even further. 

Everything you do from how you dress to crimes you've previously committed (...and got caught) are remembered or taken into account when people deal with you. Combat is what you make it; if you focus on swords, you'll excel with swords. If you're an archer, you'll be Robin Hood in no time. Focus on everything? You're a literal God ... with a rather small health bar.

Even if you've played KCD 1 and felt that it was a bit too challenging, try KCD2 -- the devs put blood, sweat, and tears into making it accessible for everyone, but still maintained the core aspect of what makes this game stand out even among the best of the best that gaming has to offer.

The narrative develops through three parts: Trosky, Kutná Hora, and the end. The tale is rich in tension, treason, and sensational scenes - the whole spectrum from the saving of Ptacek to the stunning conclusion with the coming of the allied army. Kingdom Come Deliverance II is one of those rare RPGs that feels less like a game world and more like a time machine.

From the very moment you step back into late Medieval Bohemia, the game’s commitment to the historical time period is obvious. Landscapes and towns are modeled on real locations, armour is modeled from surviving musuem pieces of that era, Peasents/nobles in towns have daily routines mapped out, heck even the night sky has been modeled to be somewhat accurate to early 1400 Bohemia.

This is not absolute however, balancing historical accuracy with enjoyability is always a tricky affair, and unless you are in the minority and you are a hard core history buff some things always get sacrificed to make the game enjoyable for all. It could be major things like there not being any children in the game at all, or smaller things like carrots anachronistically being orange. Where the dev's focused their efforts on being historically accurate they did so with spades. It’s this obsessive attention to detail that gives the game its immersibility.

Getting back into the saddle with Henry is as punishing at times as it is rewarding. 
The combat is deliberate and skill-based like the first game. Positioning, stamina, and timing matter.
Do things right and you feel like you can cleave your way through an entire army, but miss the parry or allow yourself to get riposted and you find yourself getting sent straight back to the load screen.

The continuation of Henry's story feels natural and is very well written. The game excels at making large-scale events feel personal. You’re not saving the world you’re trying to survive and find your place in it. Choices matter and the story is filled morally ambiguous choices for the player to make, and they rarely feel simple or clean.

The two regions are a big step up from the first game, The regions are overall quiet and beautiful to traverse, the notable fortresses are very well detailed internally as well as externelly but these pail in comparison to the standout location Kuttenberg. A bustling silver-mining city and economic hub, packed with shops, guilds, quests, and citizens which make the city feel dense and alive. These elements come together to make Kuttenberg arguably one of the most detailed cities ever built in an RPG.

Overall, KCD2 to me isn't just a sequel, it’s a refinement of a very specific vision. A grounded, historically rooted RPG that prioritizes immersion. One that if you’re willing to embrace, it will offer you one of the most authentic RPG experiences ever created.

At 129 hours at the time of writing this, I think I've seen just about all the game has to offer on a single playthrough.  That's not to say I've seen it all, as there's quite a bit of variety in the delivery and handling of much of the dialogue and missions can play out.  It's a bit hard to wrap my head around all my thoughts on the game after weeks of play, but I can safely say this has been one of the best titles I've ever played and the game was done a disservice in the 2025 awards.

The game looks great, runs great and has a solid, history influenced narrative that both keeps you moving along while at the same time giving you plenty of room to breathe and explore.  Most of the gameplay mechanics are great and the attention to detail is constant.  Voice acting is delivered well by the main cast, though there are a handful of actors that have a ton of multiple parts; a little more variety there would have been nice.  Combat is challenging and something I never truly excelled in, but, much like the first title, it is something you tend to grow into with both practical experience and in game skill growth.  The tale of frail to menace is just as strong in KCD2 as it was 1.  I also enjoyed the little mini games, alchemy and following cooking instructions was particularly intersting, though I imagine some might find tedious.

It's particularly fun to see just how many of your actions large and small impact things: little things like stinking to high hell can ruin your stealth missions as they smell you coming, wearing freshly stolen goods in front of their owner won't go unnoticed and major plot points in a few missions can change based on how thorough you are beforehand.

As far as technical issues, there were little.  One constant one I had was that all cut scenes would run at near 0 FPS until I broke and returned focus to the game; double tapping the windows key was enough for that.  Also had one CTD in my playthrough; not too shabby.

When it comes to the DLC, I'd highly recommend the complete package.  The two narrative based ones add probably 20-30 hrs of additional content and the blacksmithing one is a bit narrower in focus and a bit more open ended grindy, but if you tackle that one during your playthough it is far more enjoyable than I imagine it would have been on its own at release after beating the game before it.  There is no drop in quality throughout the title and the DLC continues that trend.

One last little point worth mentioning that you don't see much these days is how friendly the game is to pausing the title.  Mid cutscene, mid sentence in dialogue, mid combat, whatever; very convenient when interrupted by work, spouse, kid, bad weather, whatever.

This is a lot of words not necessarily saying a lot in particular, but the game warrants a thumbs up and all the praise people can heap on it, so I'm adding some more.  Get the title and enjoy it; I'd strongly recommend playing through the first one though first.  While not required (the game will use some flashbacks and dialogue to broadly fill in the player to the broad strokes of the first title), KCD2 is simply KCD1 improved, so if you're likely to enjoy 2, don't rob yourself of playing through 1.

The end.

// Review after 100% completing the game. //

[list]
[*][b]Gameplay[/b]
[/list]
The game is honestly a lot of fun, but it definitely leans heavily into realism, so I can see it not clicking with everyone. Combat is slow and deliberate, more about timing and positioning. You can't just mash buttons and expect to win. It has a noticeable smoother feel than the first game, with less clunkyness, while still maintaining the heavy, grounded feeling.

Controls felt good to me on both mouse & keyboard and controller, which was a nice surprise. There are a wide variety of mechanics to explore: alchemy and survival, gear maintenance, reputation, and crime system - and they all play a meaningful role in how your journey unfolds. The game rarely holds your hand, which is great if you like figuring things out on your own, but it also means you’ll probably mess up a few times before things begin to make sense.

Quests are easily one of the best parts. They're open-ended, with multiple ways to handle them, and rarely feel like basic "go there, kill that" filler. You can talk your way through situations, sneak around, or just force your way in, and the game actually reacts to what you do. It makes your choices feel meaningful, and sometimes the consequences don’t show up until much later.

[list]
[*][b]Story & World[/b]
[/list]
The story remains true to real historical events, which makes it believable, but it still manages to tell a more personal story through Henry. His journey is becoming more complex this time around, and your choices can have an impact on how people perceive and deal with you.

The world itself is probably one of the game's biggest strengths. It actually feels like it's alive. NPCs go about their daily routines, react to your reputation, and remember what you've done. If you cause trouble, people notice. If you build a good name for yourself, that can open doors later on. It all comes together in a way that makes the world feel alive, not just something you're passing through.

The writing is nicely balanced too. It handles the heavier historical side of things well, but still leaves room for smaller, more personal moments. Even side quests feel worthwhile, and a lot of them put you in situations where there isn't a clear "right" choice, which makes them more interesting.

[list]
[*][b]Visuals & Audio[/b]
[/list]
The game's visuals are incredible, and it's easily one of the most realistic worlds out there today. The environments are packed with detail, whether you’re walking through thick forests, muddy villages, or busy towns, and everything feels grounded and believable. The lighting and weather also play a significant role in making the world feel more alive from one moment to another.

Animations are noticeably better this time around, especially during conversations and combat. Characters feel more natural and expressive, which helps a lot during the more emotional parts of the story.

The sound design is just as solid. The small details like wind in the trees, people talking in the distance, and metal clashing are enough to draw you in without being overwhelming. The music is a perfect fit for the setting, adding to the mood when needed and never getting in the way.

[list]
[*][b]Performance & Technical Quality[/b]
[/list]
Overall, the performance is fairly good, especially considering the size and detail of the game. Frame rates stay consistent most of the time, and it feels well-optimized on modern hardware. I was getting around 80 FPS on High settings, which is honestly great for a game this big.

The game has some minor issues, such as textures popping in late or small AI issues, but nothing that really gets in the way. Compared to how the first game launched, KCD2 feels a lot more polished and stable.

[list]
[*][b]Design & Balance[/b]
[/list]
The game really leans into realism and allows you to do things your way, which can make it feel tough at first, especially if you're new to this kind of RPG. It puts a lot of emphasis on preparation and role-playing. What you wear, how you talk to people, even how you act in general all have an impact.

The game's difficulty is largely influenced by how you approach it. If take your time to train, earn money, and improve your skills, things will go much smoother. If you rush in without being prepared, things can quickly go wrong. One nice thing is that it doesn't lock you out of the main story based on your level, so you can move things forward at your own pace without being forced to do side content.

Some of the systems can feel a bit unforgiving, no doubt. But if you stick with them and give them time, it ends up being quite rewarding.

[list]
[*][b]Replayability[/b]
[/list]
Replayability is without a doubt one of the game's biggest strengths. You have a lot of freedom in how you shape Henry: whether you play him as an honorable knight, a sneaky thief, or something a bit more shady. Your style can have a significant impact on the outcome of every walkthrough.

Quests can play out in different ways, there are usually multiple ways to handle objectives, and you can interact with (or even get rid of) a lot of NPCs if you want to. Because of that, each run ends up feeling a little different. Add in how much content there is, and you’re looking at dozens, if not hundreds, of hours if you really get into it.

[list]
[*][b]Value for Price[/b]
[/list]
Great value for what you get. There's a lot of content here, and it's not just filler - it's detailed, well-constructed, and worth the time. There are few games that go as deep with immersion and player choice at this scale.

[list]
[*][b]Overall Impression & Recommendation[/b]
[/list]
In all honesty, it's a 10/10 if you're a fan of immersive RPGs. It takes what the first game did and improves on it in all the right ways, feeling more polished and detailed without losing what made it special in the first place.

That being said, it's definitely not for everyone. The game relies heavily on realism, has a slower pace, and doesn't simplify its systems, which may be a bit too much if you're used to more straightforward RPGs. But if it resonates with you, it's something special.

If you're willing to follow its rules, it can be a game that can truly stay with you.
